newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda gives Kenya ultimatum on power tariffs.
newsitem.headline: Uganda gives Kenya ultimatum on power tariffs.

text.p: Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni said on Monday he had told Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi to pay more for Ugandan electricity or lose the power supply.
"I have asked Moi to pay me according to the market price," Museveni told a news conference in Kampala in the latest turn in a row over a contract that dates back more than four decades.
"We have already lost a lot of money on these tariffs. But I am not asking for compensation for what I've lost in the past."
Under a 1954 agreement signed under British colonial rule, no provision is created for a review of tariffs on Ugandan power exports to Kenya until the year 2004. Uganda rejects the deal.
"No agreement can tell me to throw away my electricity. That agreement can go to hell," Museveni told reporters.

It was Museveni's second complaint about the low rates Kenya pays Uganda for electricity from its British-built Owen Falls Dam on the Nile in two weeks. Earlier this month Museveni said he had complained to Moi and called for a contract review.

Kenyan power authorities have previously said Uganda was unable to meet its power export obligations owing to its own fast-growing economy and Kenya had licensed other private companies to bridge any electricity supply shortfall.
Kenyan Energy Minister Darius Mbela said Kenya was willing to discuss a review of the contract because the current cost of power greatly exceeded the pricing when the deal was sealed.
The Kenya Power & Lighting Company (KP&LC) says the problem was not renegotiating the contract but a guarantee by Uganda that 30 megawatts under the contract would be exported to Kenya.
The company says Uganda has failed to meet that obligation.
Kenya has a power deficit of 50 megawatts. The system's peak demand is 670 megawatts while available capacity is 620 megawatts, according to the Kenya Power & Lighting Company.
Five planned new plants would end any shortfalls, experts said.
On Monday, Kenyan government officials declined any comment on Musevenis's latest threat.
Museveni said Kenya paid about two U.S. cents for a unit of electricity, while it cost six cents to generate the same unit.
"Moreover our people pay the equivalent of about 7.5 cents for the same unit. By comparison, the Kenyan government sells the same unit for the equivalent of nine cents," he said.
Museveni said he was awaiting Moi's response but made no reference to Kenyan charges that Uganda was unable to meet its obligations to Kenya.
